title: [A2 • Band 4.0] Bài 106: The Story of Tyrian Purple
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 106 (LEVEL A2 • BAND 4.0)

The Story of Tyrian Purple

Paragraph 1. In the ancient Mediterranean world, a special purple dye called Tyrian purple was very famous. People named it after Tyre, an old sea city in modern Lebanon. Only rich leaders and kings could wear clothes colored with this dye. Most ancient dyes came from plant roots or crushed insects, and they faded quickly in water. However, Tyrian purple came from meat-eating sea snails. Even better, this amazing color never washed out or faded in bright sunlight.

Paragraph 2. Making Tyrian purple was very slow and unpleasant work. Fishermen caught the sea snails along rocky coasts using woven baskets filled with bait. Workers then took out tiny liquid parts from inside each snail using sharp knives, or crushed small shells whole. Next, they soaked the liquid in salty water for three days and boiled it in large lead pots for ten days. The rotting snails created a terrible smell, so cities forced dye workshops to stay far away from houses.

Paragraph 3. When the snail liquid first came out, it looked completely clear like water. After workers dipped wool into the pot and hung it outside, sunlight changed the liquid from yellow to green and finally to deep purple. Because the dye stayed strong inside the wool fibers, washing never removed the color. In fact, sunlight made the purple look even darker and richer over time.

Paragraph 4. Tyrian purple was extremely costly because workers needed about 10,000 snails to make just one gram of pure dye. In ancient Rome, purple cloth cost as much as gold or silver. Roman rules allowed only the Emperor to wear clothes that were completely purple. Later, after big wars closed the old workshops in 1453, people forgot the secret recipe. Ordinary people could only buy purple clothes after 1856, when a young scientist made an artificial purple color by accident.
